newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PM PREDICTS INTEREST RATE CUT IF WAGE GROWTH IS LOW
The Prime Minister says if today's wages growth figures are in line with what the Reserve Bank regards as satisfactory, there should be a cut in interest rates.
John Howard told Sydney radio 2UE that it's up to the bank to make that decision, but he says low wage growth, combined with yesterday's low inflation figures, should indicate a cut.
Economists are expecting Bureau of Statistics figures to show wages have increased by about one per cent in the last quarter.
MAYOR TO APOLOGISE IN LOCAL PAPER
In South Australia, a letter from the Mayor of Port Lincoln, will appear in the city's local paper next week apologising for the hurt caused by his statements on multiculturalism.
Last week, Mayor Peter Davis issued a news release on Council letterhead calling for a reduction in immigration and an end to multiculturalism.
He later referred to the children of inter-racial marriages as mongrels, prompting the resignations of nine of the city's councillors.
Councillor Davis says the media blew his comments out of proportion, and despite giving the apology, he stands-by what he said, and would say it again.
TEACHER STABBING RAISES QUESTIONS
The stabbing of a teacher at Marrickville High School in Sydney yesterday has raised questions about teacher safety, and authority at school.

The Teachers' Federation says despite an appeal for teachers to contact the Education department if they feel threatened by students, teachers don't believe the department will support their complaints.

Federation President, Dennis Fitzgerald says the department has consistently questioned the authority of teachers to make decisions as to whether the learning environment is being threatened by certain students.
BUTLER REJECTS FRENCH SABOTAGE CLAIMS
Australia's ambassador to the United Nations says his French counterpart is outraged by claims that France sabotaged Australia's bid for a seat on the UN security council.
A report in the Australian newspaper claims France played a key role in lobbying international support to thwart Australia's bid.
But Richard Butler has rejected the claims.

Mr Butler says shortly after the vote which saw Australia miss out on one of two non-permanent Council seats to Sweden and Portugal, France had given every indication it would be happy to have Australia on the Council.
CHILD DEATH IN VICTORIA
Another Victorian child has died, again placing pressure on the State Human services department, about its child protection measures.
The Human Services Department was investigating the living conditions of three-year-old, Katy Bolger, who was found dead at her home at Geelong, earlier this month.
It's the third recent death of a toddler, where questions have been raised about child protection services and the Department's role protecting children in Victoria.
The Homicide Squad is investigating Katy's death, and the State Coroner says he'll hold a special inquiry into the deaths of children under State care or protection.
The Human Services Department says staff had been notified of concerns surrounding Katy Bolger's conditions, and had made an initial visit.
STUDY RECOMMENDS METHADONE PROGRAMMES
A study on drug addiction in South Australia is recommending methadone programs be expanded because of their economic, social, and health benefits.
The report, being prepared for the Federal Government, says in South Australia, more than half-a-million dollars a day is spent by addicts on heroin, and most of that money comes from crime.
Author, Adelaide university pharmacologist Jason White says methadone programs only cost around two-thousand dollars per person per year.
Dr White says most methadone users stop committing crimes, leading to a big drop in the number of offences such as house break-ins.
He says the programs also prevent the spread of needle transmitted diseases.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY HEARS CONFLICTING SUGGESTIONS

A suggestion that a Blackhawk helicopter took a wrong bearing, putting it in the flight path of the two helicopters which crashed has been rejected at the Military Inquiry into the June Blackhawk disaster.
The aircrew of Blackhawk five has told the Townsville hearing that its helicopter was the only aircraft on track during the counter terrorism exercise in which 18 soldiers were killied.
Sergeant Michael Allen, a loadmaster on Blackhawk five says he saw Blackhawk one and two, and they were very close to them before the explosion.
Sergeant Allen rejected claims by counsel for the pilot of Blackhawk two, Wing Commander Bob Douglas, that it was blackhawk five which was in the wrong position.
Wing commander Douglas argued Blackhawk five had taken its bearing off the wrong infra-red light.
